newsitem.title: CHINA: China's B shares fall as A share bulls run on.
newsitem.headline: China's B shares fall as A share bulls run on.

text.p: China's foreign currency B shares are continuing to perform poorly despite a strong bullrun on the domestic A share markets, and analysts on Friday blamed poor company results and restrictive measures from Beijing.

Foreign investors are mostly sellers of the B shares in Shanghai and Shenzhen and even local Chinese investors, until recently the main support for the markets, have backed off following rulings that they must buy no more B shares.

But the A share markets, with shares denominated in the local Chinese currency, have risen strongly since April this year, and analysts are predicting a continued strong run through to the middle of next year.
On Friday, Shanghai B shares ended at 48.286 points, almost unchanged from the beginning of the year while Shanghai's A share index stood at 956.166 points, up 72 percent in the same period.
Shenzhen B shares have done better and closed at 89.89 points on Friday, up 51 percent since the beginning of the year.
But they are still far below the Shenzhen A share index which has soared 170 percent during the past nine months and ended at Friday at 314.88.
The Shenzhen B share index has performed better than Shanghai in 1996 because the companies listed there posted better results than their counterparts in Shanghai, a domestic broker said.
"Most foreign investors have lost confidence in China's B share firms given their worsening results over the past two years," said an analyst with the Guotai Securities.
The reported profits for most B shares companies declined in the 1995 full year and the first half of 1996, even those of former blue chips such as Yaohua Pilkington and Shanghai Shangling.
Yaohua Pilkington posted a half-year net profit of 54.81 million yuan, down 61.5 percent from the same 1995 period, and Shangling's net profit was down 53 percent.
A foreign broker said most foreign brokers had revised their forecasts for B share firms down and most foreign investors had sold their positions and left the markets.

The securities authorities have taken a wide range of measures in recent months to boost confidence in the A share markets, including this week a decision to allow mutual funds to be listed on the markets.
But the B share markets have mostly been negatively affected by recent edicts from Beijing, analysts said.

The China Securities Regulation Commission has repeatedly stressed that domestic investors are banned from trading B shares, largely to stop the outflow of foreign exchange as foreign investors sell into domestic demand, analysts said.
But they said the authorities were unable to force the domestic investors out of the market completely, or else B share prices would collapse.
One trader said trading by domestic investors currently still accounted for about 50 percent of B share volume in Shanghai and a little more than that in Shenzhen.

Given the restrictions from Beijing, foreign investors remain cautious about the B shares markets even though the B share companies are expected to perform better over the next few months, the analysts said.
